chapter_theme: The paalai decade of Kannan Senthanar: the man leaves for wealth across a waste of fire, stone, bowmen and vultures (11, 12, 15, 17, 18, 19), the woman watches her bangles and colour fail while the season he swore by comes (13, 14), and the lovers elope, the man praising the road and the mother fearing it (16, 20).

11.reading: Gossip aside, the speaker tells the woman with eyes like washed blue lilies that her lover, whose nature is set on wealth, broke his word and left for a wasteland where the waters have perished, the heat rises shimmering, and the water along the way is cut off.
11.nuance: பொய்த்தனர் and நீத்தார் stand side by side: the lie and the leaving are one act. The water named three times (அழிநீர, வழிநீர் and the lily of கழுநீர்) sets her watered eyes against the land that has lost its water.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless wasteland he crossed for wealth

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): a woman is addressed by her eyes, most likely by the friend; the heroine speaking to the friend is possible

12.reading: To the man setting out for the wealth he hopes to gain across a forest where fire has spread and the land, strewn with broken pebbles, has lost its nature, the speaker says that when it comes to weighing it, no one can know better than he the helplessness of the woman whose kohl-dark eyes are streaked with red.
12.nuance: The closing question flatters and accuses at once: he, her intimate, knows her grief best, so if he goes he goes knowing. The ruined land (முரண் அழிந்து, its strength or nature destroyed) foreshadows what his going will do to her.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is about to leave for wealth through the burnt forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the friend speaks to the departing man of the heroine's ஆற்றாமை, to hold him back

13.reading: The tall kurunthu has budded, beside it the maraa has bloomed, and glory lilies have come out among them; now, O you with golden bangles, the koel has turned into a lie every word he swore when he joined us and went.
13.nuance: The season of the flowers is the season he named, so the koel's call is the proof that his oath failed; the poem blames the bird for making the words false, a displacement that spares the man's name. Read the other way, the koel's call is itself false, a season come too soon, and the line consoles; the verse is marked uncertain for that reason.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits at home past the season he swore to return by, which is the situation of irutthal

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the woman whose man has not come in the promised season speaks to her gold-bangled friend

14.reading: Even after seeing the season when the red-eyed koel calls through every cool flowering grove where the punnai opens its puffed-rice blossoms, he left her, driven by his heart's craving for wealth; yet her heart keeps watching for his coming.
14.nuance: Two cravings are set in the same word: his நசை for wealth that drove him off and her heart's நசை for his return. கண்டும், 'even seeing', makes his leaving a choice made against the season of love.

thinai_evidence.note: he left for wealth in spring, and she bears the parting

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the woman speaks of her own heart; the friend is the likely hearer

comparisons.tenor: the beauty of her body before the pallor

15.reading: The woman asks her friend whether the man, who gave up grace for the craving of hard-won wealth while her body, lovely as tender leaves, grows pale, is now halting somewhere on the long wasteland of hard paths, where the little hawk rages at the small dull dove.
15.nuance: Reproach and worry share one sentence: he abandoned grace (அருள் ஒழிந்து), yet she wonders where he lodges tonight. The hawk at the dove is the road's violence; it could be read as his harshness to the meek, but no act of a lover is in it and the deletion of line 1 takes nothing she says, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: he is away on the long waste for wealth while she pales

comparisons.tenor: her small new teeth, like buds

16.reading: The man tells the shy girl with sweet speech and newly budded sharp teeth that the place they are going to is one to be wished for, now that the dark-trunked maraa blooms together with the nuna and swarms of broad-winged bees hum the paalai melody.
16.nuance: The bees hum பாலை, the music named for the very land the lovers must cross, so the man turns the dreaded landscape into a song to lead her on. The verse never names the road's hardship; its comfort is all in what it leaves out.

thinai_evidence.note: the lovers set out together, leaving her home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the man reassures the girl as they set out together (உடன்போக்கு)

17.reading: The woman wonders whether our man, who left without grace for love of wealth while her soft shoulders with their bright bangles grew slack, will pass even through the hamlets of those who live by ploughing with the bow, where at the mouth of the stony track the black thudi drum sounds and toddy flows.
17.nuance: வில்லுழுது வாழ்நர், 'those who live by ploughing with the bow', is the bandit's livelihood named as a farmer's, which makes the threat sound settled and ordinary. நமர், 'our man', keeps him hers even in the sentence that calls him graceless.

thinai_evidence.note: the stony track and the bow-living hamlets of the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the woman speaks of 'our man' (நமர்), so to her friend

18.reading: For the man going to the wide forest where tangled bamboo, its nodes split by the scorching sun, sheds pearls, the speaker's bangles do not look like ones that will meet his return; every one of them seems ready to fall, for nothing.
18.nuance: The bamboo sheds its pearls in the heat as her bangles are about to fall from her thinning arms: the land drops its treasure on the road he takes for wealth while she loses her ornaments uselessly (கொன்னே). Line 3 is hard to construe, so the verse is marked uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-scorched wide forest he travels

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the woman speaks of her own bangles

comparisons.tenor: the pallor spreading over her breasts

iraicchi.act: the doe and the stag cry out together in the parched track, sharing its hardship instead of parting
iraicchi.sense: even the deer of the waste keep together in distress, while he faces the road alone and she wilts alone at home

19.reading: The woman asks her friend whether he, afraid of the stony desert track where the doe cries out with the stag, will halt somewhere in the long wasteland; alas, the gold colour that wilts down over her breasts, and her shoulders, slip away together with her bangles.
19.nuance: Three things droop together, the pallor with the breasts and the shoulders with the bangles, matching the pair of deer that suffer together on his road: in the waste even the beasts keep each other company, while he and she wilt apart.

thinai_evidence.note: the stony desert road he is on

comparisons.tenor: the young man with the strong bow

20.reading: The mother asks a passing man whether her daughter can bear to walk, beside the young man with a strong bow fierce as Death, across the harsh wasteland of the Eyinar with their strung bows, where flocks of vultures gather and she will shrink in fear from the shadows they cast.
20.nuance: The youth she went with is himself likened to Death (கூற்றின), so the mother finds no safety even in the girl's protector; the question is whether the girl can bear it (ஆற்றுங்கொல்), not whether she will come back.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has gone off with the youth across the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the mother (என்மகள்) asks a man met on the road (ஐய) after her eloped daughter; she may be the foster mother

links.note: Kural 1151, the friend (for Parimelazhagar) to the departing man: tell me if you are not going; tell your quick return to those still alive then. Thinaimozhi 12, the friend to the man leaving for wealth: who can know her helplessness better than you?
links.teaches: Holding them together shows two moves in the friend's attempt to stop the journey: the couplet threatens with the woman's death, while the venba appeals to the man's own knowledge of her, making him the witness who cannot claim ignorance.

links.note: Akananuru 229: the girl answers her friend that the man who promised to come at once has not come even in young spring, when the koel calls on the budding branch. Thinaimozhi 13: the flowering season has come and the koel has made all his sworn words false.
links.teaches: The Akananuru lets the koel mark the date the promise failed, while the venba makes the koel the agent that turns his oath into a lie, so the four-line form compresses the long poem's reasoning into a single accusation aimed at the bird instead of the man.

links.note: Kural 1264: thinking of the return of the man who left the love they shared, her heart climbs up as on branches. Thinaimozhi 14: though he left for wealth even after seeing the koel's season, her heart watches for his coming.
links.teaches: The couplet's heart rising in hope of his return gains in the venba a bitter premise, that he chose to leave in the very season of love, so the longing is shown to persist against her knowledge of his choice, not out of ignorance of it.

links.note: Akananuru 375: the girl tells her friend her eyes would not weep if she knew the man who crossed the wasteland of killers would return unharmed. Thinaimozhi 15: she asks her friend whether the man who gave up grace for wealth halts on the long waste where the hawk attacks the dove.
links.teaches: In Akananuru 375 fear for his safety is the whole cause of her tears, but the venba puts that fear in the same sentence as the charge that he abandoned grace, showing that the heroine's worry for him survives her own accusation against him.

links.note: Natrinai 9: the eloping man tells the white-toothed girl to go without strain, lingering at every shade, since the road they take (யாம் செல்லும் ஆறே) runs through cool groves where the koel calls. Thinaimozhi 16: he tells the girl with budding teeth that the place they go (நாம் செல்லும் இடம்) is to be desired, as maraa blooms and bees hum.
links.teaches: Both men answer the girl's fear of the waste by describing its blossoms, which shows a fixed speech of the eloping lover; the venba's own turn is to have the bees hum the paalai melody, turning the name of the dreaded land into the music that leads her across it.

links.note: Akananuru 355: in spring bees hum on the budding branches like the strings of a paalai lute touched by a master, the season in which the heroine fears her man's going. Thinaimozhi 16: bees hum the paalai melody as the man leads the girl away.
links.teaches: The same sound of bees playing the paalai mode marks the spring of a parting in the Akananuru and the spring of an elopement in the venba, so the image does not carry a fixed mood but takes its grief or its promise from the uri it serves.

links.note: Kural 872: take on the enmity of ploughmen whose plough is the bow rather than of those whose plough is the word. Thinaimozhi 17: the woman fears for her man passing the hamlets of those who live by ploughing with the bow, while her shoulders slacken because he left without grace.
links.teaches: The Kural ranks the bow-ploughmen as the lesser enemy, and the venba agrees in its own way: the bowmen are only a feared danger on his road, while the wound she actually bears, slackened shoulders, comes from his word, the promise and grace he withheld.

links.note: Akananuru 185: her bright bangles slip as the man crosses summer hills where seed-bearing bamboo bursts with the twang of warriors' bows. Thinaimozhi 18: on the road where sun-split bamboo sheds pearls, her bangles seem ready to fall.
links.teaches: In the Akananuru the bursting bamboo is a sound of violence on his road, while the venba makes the same bursting shed pearls, a treasure dropped in the land where he seeks wealth, set against her bangles falling for nothing, so the image of the split bamboo is turned from danger to the waste of what is precious.

links.note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone her shoulders lose their old beauty and fullness and the bangles slip. Thinaimozhi 19: the woman, picturing him halting in the stony waste where the doe cries with the stag, says her shoulders slip with her bangles.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the wasting shoulders as the plain sign of absence, and the venba supplies what she is thinking of while they waste: his fear on the road and the paired deer that keep together, so the symptom is tied to an imagined scene rather than to absence alone.

links.note: Natrinai 279: the mother asks whether the feet of her jewelled girl, her anklets removed, are weary on the sun-glittering track. Thinaimozhi 20: the mother asks a man on the road whether her daughter can bear to walk the harsh waste with a youth whose bow is like Death.
links.teaches: Natrinai's mother fears only the road and the girl's tender feet, but the venba's mother fears the companion too, calling him Death-like, which shows the mother's grief can doubt the very youth the girl trusted for protection.

source_issues: 11 line 1: repaired from ெ + ள to ௌ (கௌவையோ); the sangamtamil.com text lacks line 1.
11 line 3: அழிநீர் வாகி reads as அழிநீர ஆகி (compare 12 line 1, முரிபரல வாகி); the line's sense (water perished, heat rising) is uncertain, and the verse is marked uncertain.
17 line 3: எல்வனை is very likely a misprint for எல்வளை, bright bangle (compare Akananuru 185 line 1, எல்வளை ஞெகிழ).
18 line 3: எதிர்வன போல்இலவே is hard to construe; it is taken as 'they do not look like bangles that will meet his return', and the verse is marked uncertain.
13 line 4: whether the koel proves his words false or is itself false (calling before the season) cannot be fixed; the verse is marked uncertain.
